addmaths-0606-logs-bases-and-powers.description: Convert between powers and logarithms. Use positive arguments, including fractional and negative powers.

sections.title: What does a logarithm return?
sections.label: Inverse powers
sections.intro: Read a log statement as a question about an exponent. For a legal base, each positive argument has one corresponding power.

sections.title: Can the base be the unknown?

sections.title: Which arguments are allowed?

sections.intro: A positive real base raised to any real power always gives a positive result. The inverse logarithm therefore needs its argument to be positive.

examples.title: Read a logarithm as a power
examples.question:
A scale uses the base \(16\).

  1. Give the exact value of \(\log_{16}\left(64\right)\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact increase in the logarithm when the argument changes to \(256\).

    [2]
solution: (a) Write the base and argument as powers of \(4\).
If the logarithm is \(x\), then \(4^{(2)x}=4^{3}\). Match exponents.
(b) The new exponent in base \(4\) is \(4\).

revision.body:
What does a logarithm return?

The statements \(b^u=v\) and \(\log_{b}\left(v\right)=u\) have the same meaning when \(b>0,\ b\ne1,\ v>0\).

Can the base be the unknown?

For unknown positive \(b\), \(\log_{b}\left(v\right)=u\) gives \(b=v^{1/u}\) if \(u\ne0\) and the answer is a legal base.

Which arguments are allowed?

For a logarithm of a whole expression, require that whole expression to be greater than zero, for example \(\lg(5x-1)\) needs \(x>\tfrac15\).

addmaths-0606-logs-log-laws.description: Use the product, quotient and power laws to combine and evaluate logarithms.

sections.title: Why does subtraction divide the arguments?
sections.label: Quotient law
sections.intro: Dividing powers of the same number subtracts their exponents. Logarithms return those exponents.

blocks.html: With positive arguments \(A,B\), \(\log_{b}\left(A\right)-\log_{b}\left(B\right)=\log_{b}\left(\tfrac{A}{B}\right)\).

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(L=\log_{4}\left(2048\right)-\log_{4}\left(8\right)\).

Evaluate L exactly.
blocks.hint: Divide the two positive arguments before evaluating the logarithm.
blocks.solution:
The difference of logs has argument \(\frac{2048}{8}=256\).

Since \(4^{4}=256\), the logarithm is \(4\).

\(4\)

blocks.html: Subtracting the arguments gives a different number. Form the quotient first.

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(L=\log_{6}\left(10368\right)-\log_{6}\left(8\right)\).

Evaluate L exactly.
blocks.hint: Divide the two positive arguments before evaluating the logarithm.
blocks.solution:
The difference of logs has argument \(\frac{10368}{8}=1296\).

Since \(6^{4}=1296\), the logarithm is \(4\).

\(4\)

blocks.html: Keep the order of arguments: the subtracted log supplies the denominator.

sections.title: How can I write several terms as one log?
sections.label: Power product
sections.intro: First move an outside coefficient to a power of the argument. Then join same-base logs by multiplying or dividing arguments.

blocks.html: Use \(n\log_{b}\left(x\right)=\log_{b}\left(x^n\right)\) before applying the product and quotient laws. Each original argument must be positive.

blocks.prompt:
For \(x>0\), consider \(2\log_{5}\left(x\right)+\log_{5}\left(3\right)-\log_{5}\left(3\right)\).

Write this expression as a single logarithm to base \(5\).
blocks.hint: Use the power law, then combine the arguments with the product and quotient laws.
blocks.solution:
Move \(2\) into the exponent of \(x\), giving \(\log_{5}\left(x^2\right)\).

Multiply the first two arguments and divide by \(3\).

\(\log_{5}\left(x^2\right)\)

blocks.html: No log law replaces a logarithm of a sum by a sum of logarithms.

blocks.prompt:
For \(x>0\), consider \(2\log_{7}\left(x\right)+\log_{7}\left(3\right)-\log_{7}\left(3\right)\).

Write this expression as a single logarithm to base \(7\).
blocks.hint: Use the power law, then combine the arguments with the product and quotient laws.
blocks.solution:

Multiply the first two arguments and divide by \(3\).

\(\log_{7}\left(x^2\right)\)

blocks.html: For symbolic arguments, write the combined argument clearly before simplifying it.

sections.title: Can I evaluate the logs before using a law?
sections.label: Integer powers
sections.intro: When an argument is a familiar power of the base, you can evaluate the log directly and then do the arithmetic.

blocks.html: If \(A=b^u\) and \(B=b^v\), then \(k\log_{b}\left(A\right)-\log_{b}\left(B\right)=ku-v\).

blocks.prompt:
The value \(D\) is defined by \(D=3\log_{3}\left(9\right)-\log_{3}\left(81\right)\).

Evaluate D exactly.
blocks.hint: Evaluate each logarithm as an exponent before applying the outside coefficient.
blocks.solution:
The individual logarithms are \(2\) and \(4\).

Substitute into the expression to get \(3\times2-4=2\).

\(2\)

retry.feedback: The coefficient multiplies the entire first logarithm.

blocks.html: The coefficient multiplies the value of its own logarithm. It does not multiply the log base.

examples.title: Use the quotient law before evaluating
examples.question:
Consider \(L=\log_{3}\left(648\right)-\log_{3}\left(8\right)\).

  1. Evaluate L exactly.

    [2]

  2. Find the value of \(\log_{3}\left(8\right)+L\) as a single logarithm to base \(3\).

    [2]
solution: (a) The difference of logs has argument \(\frac{648}{8}=81\).
Adding logarithms with the same base multiplies their arguments.

examples.title: Use the quotient law before evaluating
examples.question:

    [2]

    [2]
solution: (a) The difference of logs has argument \(\frac{256}{8}=32\).
Adding logarithms with the same base multiplies their arguments.

examples.title: Combine three logarithms into one
examples.question:
For \(x>0\), consider \(2\log_{4}\left(x\right)+\log_{4}\left(3\right)-\log_{4}\left(3\right)\).

  1. Write this expression as a single logarithm to base \(4\).

    [2]

  2. Solve the equation obtained by setting the original expression equal to \(\log_{4}\left(4\right)\).

    [2]
solution: (a) Move \(2\) into the exponent of \(x\), giving \(\log_{4}\left(x^2\right)\).
Multiply the first two arguments and divide by \(3\).
(b) Logarithms with the same legal base are one-to-one.
Equate the arguments, cancel their common coefficient and solve \(x^2=4\). Keep the positive value.

addmaths-0606-logs-change-of-base.description: Use a common base, work with given log values and interpret reciprocals.

sections.title: How do I choose a better base?
sections.label: Same base
sections.intro: Turn the log into an exponential equation, take logs in a new base, then solve for the original exponent. A base shared by both numbers can give an exact rational result.

blocks.html: For any legal new base \(c\), \(\log_{a}\left(b\right)=\frac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}\).

blocks.prompt:
The two numbers used in a scaling rule are \(A=117649\) and \(B=16807\).

Find \(\log_{A}\left(B\right)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use the same new base above and below the fraction.
blocks.solution:
Changing to base \(7\) gives \(\frac{\log_{7}\left(B\right)}{\log_{7}\left(A\right)}\).

The numerator is \(5\) and the denominator is \(6\).

\(\frac{5}{6}\)

retry.feedback: You calculated the logarithm in reverse order. The denominator is the log of the original base.

blocks.html: Apply the same new base to numerator and denominator. The original base is in the denominator.

blocks.prompt:
The two numbers used in a scaling rule are \(A=531441\) and \(B=59049\).

Find \(\log_{A}\left(B\right)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use the same new base above and below the fraction.
blocks.solution:
Changing to base \(9\) gives \(\frac{\log_{9}\left(B\right)}{\log_{9}\left(A\right)}\).

The numerator is \(5\) and the denominator is \(6\).

\(\frac{5}{6}\)

retry.feedback: You calculated the logarithm in reverse order. The denominator is the log of the original base.

blocks.html: Choose a common small base if both numbers are powers of it.

sections.title: How can I use given logs without evaluating the numbers?
sections.label: Given log values
sections.intro: A problem might give the logarithms of two variables. Use these values directly in the change-of-base ratio.

blocks.html: The numerator of \(\log_{b}\left(a^n\right)\) after changing to base 10 is \(\lg(a^n)=n\lg a\).

blocks.prompt:
Positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) satisfy \(\lg a=11,\quad \lg b=2\).

Find \(\log_{b}\left(a^6\right)\) without evaluating \(a\) or \(b\).
blocks.hint: Write one ratio in base 10 and apply the power law to the numerator.
blocks.solution:
Change to base 10. The numerator becomes \(6\lg a\) using the power law.

Divide \(66\) by \(2\).

\(33\)

retry.feedback: The argument is a power of a. Its logarithm contains the extra exponent as a multiplier.

blocks.html: Include the power as a multiplier after changing the base.

blocks.prompt:
Positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) satisfy \(\lg a=3,\quad \lg b=3\).

Find \(\log_{b}\left(a^6\right)\) without evaluating \(a\) or \(b\).
blocks.hint: Write one ratio in base 10 and apply the power law to the numerator.
blocks.solution:
Change to base 10. The numerator becomes \(6\lg a\) using the power law.

Divide \(18\) by \(3\).

\(6\)

retry.feedback: The argument is a power of a. Its logarithm contains the extra exponent as a multiplier.

blocks.html: Keep the ratio exact until the required answer is obtained.

sections.title: What does the reciprocal of a logarithm mean?
sections.label: Reciprocal
sections.intro: If you swap which value is the log base and which is the argument, all the terms in the base-change ratio swap.

blocks.html: When \(a,b>0\) and both differ from 1, \(\frac{1}{\log_{a}\left(b\right)}=\log_{b}\left(a\right)\).

blocks.prompt:
Here a reciprocal means the number 1 divided by the logarithm. Let \(R=\frac{1}{\log_{9}\left(27\right)}\).

Find R exactly.
blocks.hint: Find the base-change ratio, then invert the fraction.
blocks.solution:
The inner log is \(\frac{3}{2}\) because \(9\) and \(27\) are powers of \(3\).

Invert this value, or interchange the base and the argument using change of base.

\(\frac{2}{3}\)

retry.feedback: This is the logarithm itself. The displayed expression is its reciprocal.

blocks.html: A reciprocal is a fraction with numerator 1. It is different from an inverse function.

blocks.prompt:
Here a reciprocal means the number 1 divided by the logarithm. Let \(R=\frac{1}{\log_{25}\left(125\right)}\).

Find R exactly.
blocks.hint: Find the base-change ratio, then invert the fraction.
blocks.solution:
The inner log is \(\frac{3}{2}\) because \(25\) and \(125\) are powers of \(5\).

Invert this value, or interchange the base and the argument using change of base.

\(\frac{2}{3}\)

retry.feedback: This is the logarithm itself. The displayed expression is its reciprocal.

blocks.html: Check that the original logarithm is nonzero before taking its reciprocal.

The two numbers used in a scaling rule are \(A=46656\) and \(B=7776\).

examples.title: Use known logarithms as data
examples.question:
Positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) satisfy \(\lg a=10,\quad \lg b=2\).

  1. Find \(\log_{b}\left(a^6\right)\) without evaluating \(a\) or \(b\).

    [2]

  2. Evaluate \(\log_{a}\left(b^6\right)\) exactly.

examples.title: Simplify a reciprocal of a logarithm
examples.question:
Here a reciprocal means the number 1 divided by the logarithm. Let \(R=\frac{1}{\log_{4}\left(8\right)}\).

  1. Find R exactly.

    [2]

  2. Verify that \(\log_{8}\left(4\right)\) equals R using a common base.

    [2]
solution: (a) The inner log is \(\frac{3}{2}\) because \(4\) and \(8\) are powers of \(2\).
Invert this value, or interchange the base and the argument using change of base.
(b) Write the new base as \(2^{3}\) and the argument as \(2^{2}\).

revision.body:
How do I choose a better base?

For any legal new base \(c\), \(\log_{a}\left(b\right)=\frac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}\).

How can I use given logs without evaluating the numbers?

The numerator of \(\log_{b}\left(a^n\right)\) after changing to base 10 is \(\lg(a^n)=n\lg a\).

What does the reciprocal of a logarithm mean?

When \(a,b>0\) and both differ from 1, \(\frac{1}{\log_{a}\left(b\right)}=\log_{b}\left(a\right)\).

sections.title: How do I start with one logarithm?
sections.label: Single log
sections.intro: State the restriction first. Convert the log equality into exponential form. Then solve the simpler algebraic equation and check the original argument.

blocks.html: Use \(\log_{a}\left(U\right)=r\) to obtain \(U=a^r\). The function requires \(U>0\).

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(\log_{2}\left(7x-3\right)=4\).

Find the exact solution.
blocks.hint: Rewrite in exponential form and solve the resulting linear equation.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite the equation as \(7x-3=16\).

Add \(3\) and divide by \(7\). The argument is \(16\), so it is positive.

\(x=\frac{19}{7}\)

retry.feedback: The linear expression subtracts the constant. Add that constant to both sides before dividing.

blocks.html: The right-hand side of the new equation is a power of the log base.

blocks.hint: Rewrite in exponential form and solve the resulting linear equation.

Add \(3\) and divide by \(7\). The argument is \(256\), so it is positive.

\(x=37\)

sections.title: Which root of the product equation is valid?
sections.label: Products roots
sections.intro: Combine same-base logarithms into one. The resulting product can be positive even when both individual arguments are negative.

blocks.html: A solution must make each original argument positive. The condition \(UV>0\) alone is weaker than \(U>0\) and \(V>0\) together.

blocks.prompt:
Solve \(\log_{6}\left(x-12\right)+\log_{6}\left(x+1283\right)=4\) over the reals.

Give the valid solution.
blocks.hint: Combine the logarithms as a product and solve the quadratic.
blocks.solution:
Both arguments must be positive. The stronger restriction is \(x>12\).

Combine the logs and solve \((x-12)(x+1283)=1296\).

The candidates are \(13\) and \(-1284\). Only \(13\) satisfies the restriction.

\(x=13\)

retry.feedback: That root solves the product equation, but the individual log arguments are not positive.

blocks.html: Do not accept a quadratic root without testing the original arguments.

blocks.prompt:
Solve \(\log_{2}\left(x-13\right)+\log_{2}\left(x-12\right)=1\) over the reals.

Give the valid solution.
blocks.hint: Combine the logarithms as a product and solve the quadratic.
blocks.solution:
Both arguments must be positive. The stronger restriction is \(x>13\).

Combine the logs and solve \((x-13)(x-12)=2\).

The candidates are \(14\) and \(11\). Only \(14\) satisfies the restriction.

\(x=14\)

retry.feedback: That root solves the product equation, but the individual log arguments are not positive.

blocks.html: Write a rejection reason beside any candidate you exclude.

sections.title: How can I handle subtraction or different bases?
sections.label: Quotients bases
sections.intro: A difference of same-base logs gives a quotient. If the bases differ, change to a common base before combining any terms.

blocks.html: Set the quotient of the original arguments to \(a^r\) when their log difference in base \(a\) equals \(r\). Check that the denominator is positive.

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(\log_{4}\left(19x-22\right)-\log_{4}\left(x-1\right)=2\).

Find the exact value of x.
blocks.hint: Use the quotient law and solve the resulting linear equation.
blocks.solution:
The original arguments require \(x>\frac{22}{19}\) and \(x>1\).

Combine to a quotient and rearrange to \(19x-22=16(x-1)\).

Collect like terms. At \(2\), the arguments are \(16\) and \(1\), so the value is valid.

\(2\)

blocks.html: Cross-multiplying before noting the domain can introduce candidates excluded by an original argument.

blocks.prompt:
Consider \(\log_{6}\left(39x-42\right)-\log_{6}\left(x-1\right)=2\).

Find the exact value of x.
blocks.hint: Use the quotient law and solve the resulting linear equation.
blocks.solution:
The original arguments require \(x>\frac{14}{13}\) and \(x>1\).

Combine to a quotient and rearrange to \(39x-42=36(x-1)\).

Collect like terms. At \(2\), the arguments are \(36\) and \(1\), so the value is valid.

\(2\)

blocks.html: At the end, substitute to confirm that both log arguments are positive.

sections.title: When can I match the exponents?
sections.label: Matching bases
sections.intro: Look for a small common base before taking any logarithms. Since legal exponential functions pass each positive value once, equal outputs give equal exponents.

blocks.html: If \(b>0\) and \(b\ne1\), then \(b^u=b^v\) implies \(u=v\).

blocks.prompt:
The equation is \(625^{2x+1}=625^{6}\).

Find x exactly.
blocks.hint: Use a shared base and equate the two exponents.
blocks.solution:
Write the two bases as powers of \(5\).

Equate the exponents to get \(4(2x+1)=24\). Solve for \(x\).

\(\frac{5}{2}\)

retry.feedback: The outside power multiplies both terms of the inner exponent.

blocks.html: When changing the base of a power, multiply the entire exponent by the extra power.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.html: State the common base in your working, then solve a linear equation if possible.

sections.title: What if the bases do not match?
sections.label: Unmatched bases
sections.intro: Isolate the term with the unknown exponent. Take logarithms of both sides so the power law makes that exponent a multiplier.

blocks.html: For \(a>0\), \(a\ne1\) and \(b>0\), the solution of \(a^x=b\) is \(x=\frac{\ln b}{\ln a}\).

blocks.prompt:

Give the value of x correct to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Take logs of both sides and bring the exponent down.
blocks.solution:
Take natural logarithms of both sides, giving \((3x+1)\ln 7=\ln 27\).

Collect the terms to get \(x=\frac{\ln 27-\ln 7}{3\ln 7}\). Round at the end.

\(x\approx 0.231\)

blocks.html: If a constant has been added outside the exponential, move it before taking logs.

sections.title: When is an expression a disguised quadratic?
sections.label: Substitute
sections.intro: When one exponential term is the square of another, replace the smaller one with a positive variable. Solve the quadratic, then convert back.

blocks.html: With \(u=a^x\), the expression \(a^{2x}\) becomes \(u^2\) and \(u>0\).

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Substitute a single positive variable for the basic exponential.

\(x=-1\text{ or }x=0\)

examples.title: Solve by rewriting two powers in one base

The equation is \(256^{2x+1}=256^{6}\).

  1. Find x exactly.

    [2]

  2. Hence solve \(256^{2x+1}=256^{7}\) exactly.

solution: (a) Write the two bases as powers of \(4\).
Equate the exponents to get \(4(2x+1)=24\). Solve for \(x\).
(b) The exponent on the right increases by \(4\) in base \(4\).
The exponent on the left grows by \(8\) per unit of \(x\).

examples.title: Solve an exponential equation with logarithms
examples.question:
Consider the equation \(6^{3x+1}=27\).

  1. Give the value of x correct to 3 decimal places.

    [3]

  2. If the right-hand side is multiplied by \(6\), by how much does the solution increase? Give an exact value.

    [2]
solution: (a) Take natural logarithms of both sides, giving \((3x+1)\ln 6=\ln 27\).
Collect the terms to get \(x=\frac{\ln 27-\ln 6}{3\ln 6}\). Round at the end.
(b) Multiplying the output by the base \(6\) increases the exponent by 1.
Since the exponent has gradient \(3\), x increases by \(\frac{1}{3}\).

revision.body:
When can I match the exponents?

If \(b>0\) and \(b\ne1\), then \(b^u=b^v\) implies \(u=v\).

What if the bases do not match?

For \(a>0\), \(a\ne1\) and \(b>0\), the solution of \(a^x=b\) is \(x=\frac{\ln b}{\ln a}\).

When is an expression a disguised quadratic?

With \(u=a^x\), the expression \(a^{2x}\) becomes \(u^2\) and \(u>0\).

sections.title: How can I find a multiplier from two observations?
sections.label: Recover model
sections.intro: In a multiplicative model the same positive factor applies over equal time intervals. Divide the later observation by the earlier one to cancel the scale.

blocks.html: For \(P(t)=Ab^t\), the ratio over \(\Delta t\) time units is \(b^{\Delta t}\). The positive root recovers b.

TimeReading

\(5\)\(\frac{2737152}{3125}\)

The ratio is \(\frac{20736}{625}\), so take its positive \(4\)th root.

sections.title: When does a decaying measurement reach a known level?
sections.label: Threshold
sections.intro: Find the time at which the reading equals its target. Isolate the exponential first. If the model approaches a non-zero background level, subtract that level before dividing.

blocks.html: For \(R=Ae^{-kt}\) with \(A,k>0\), set \(R=L\). Then \(e^{-kt}=\dfrac{L}{A}\), so \(t=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{A}{L}\right)}{k}\). A target can be reached at \(t\geq0\) only when \(0<L\leq A\). For \(R=B+Ae^{-kt}\), apply the same method to the amount above \(B\), which is \(L-B\) at the target.

blocks.prompt:
A sensor records \(R=22e^{-\frac{1}{5}t}\) for time t in hours. The alert level is \(\frac{11}{2}\).

Find the time at which the reading reaches the alert level. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Isolate the exponential factor and use the natural logarithm.
blocks.solution:
Divide by \(22\). This gives \(e^{-\frac{1}{5}t}=\frac{1}{4}\).

Take logs and divide by the negative coefficient of t, obtaining \(t=\frac{-\ln(\frac{1}{4})}{\frac{1}{5}}\).

\(6.931\text{ h}\)

blocks.prompt: A signal has strength \(R=32e^{-\frac{t}{5}}\) after \(t\) hours. When does its strength become \(12\) units? Give your answer in hours to 3 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Set \(R=12\), divide by the starting strength, and take natural logarithms.
blocks.solution: \[e^{-\frac{t}{5}}=\frac{12}{32}=\frac{3}{8}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t=5\ln\frac{8}{3}\approx4.904\text{ hours}.\]

blocks.html: In a decay model with a background level \(B\), the quantity \(R-B\) decays. Taking the logarithm before you isolate that quantity can select the wrong time.

blocks.solution:

\[e^{-\frac{t}{6}}=\frac{1}{4}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t=6\ln 4\approx8.318\text{ minutes}.\]

A mug of tea has temperature \(T=20+60e^{-\frac{3t}{10}}\) °C after \(t\geq0\) minutes.

    [3]

  2. According to this model, does it reach exactly \(20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) in a finite time? Explain your answer.

    [1]
solution: (a) The temperature is \(30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) above room level at the target. Subtract \(20\) from \(50\), then divide by \(60\), giving \(e^{-\frac{3t}{10}}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

  2. Find the value predicted one interval before the reference time. Explain the interpretation of this calculation.

    [2]
solution: Divide the later reading by the reference reading and take the positive \(6\)th root.
(b) Divide rather than multiply to move back one time interval.

revision.body:
How do I invert a shifted exponential?

Inverting \(y=ke^{nx}+a\) uses \(x=\frac1n\ln\left(\frac{y-a}{k}\right)\). The quotient inside ln must be positive.

How do I invert a transformed logarithm?

If \(y=k\ln(ax+b)\), then \(ax+b=e^{y/k}\). Preserve the original input restriction when giving the inverse range.

Can I evaluate the inverse without finding its whole rule?

To find \(f^{-1}(c)\), solve \(f(x)=c\). Where f is one-to-one, the equation has at most one solution.
